newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Philippine sugar 1996/97 output may top forecast.
newsitem.headline: Philippine sugar 1996/97 output may top forecast.

text.p: Philippine raw sugar output may be even higher than a forecast for two million tonnes maximum in the current production year, Jose Maria Zabaleta, executive director of the Philippine Sugar Millers Association, said.
"We are expecting a crop from 1.9 to 2.0 million tonnes. Demand is expected to be anywhere from 1.85 to 1.9 (million tonnes)," Zabeleta said in an interview.
But he did not rule out even higher production.
"Indicators are that it will be a very good crop, so, we just might exceed two million," he added.
It is still quite early in the current September-August production year, he said, but added so far factors have been favourable.
Zabaleta spoke with Reuters during a visit here with Pedro Roxas, chairman of the Philippine Sugar Millers Association, and chief executive of Central Azucarera Don Pedro.
Zabaleta said sugar content in the current crop is high, and recent rains should also be positive for production.
German firm F.O. Licht is estimating 1.9 million tonnes for the current production year, and puts 1995/1996 raw 1995/96 output at 1.775 million tonnes.
Zabaleta said it was too early to say whether the Philippines, where sugar consumption has been rising, will need to import sugar this year.

"We have an overhang of about, possibly even 300,000 tonnes from the last crop year. So we are uncertain at the moment if there will be some imports to cover up for the export committments, or whether we will be in balance. It is too early in the crop year to determine that," he said.
In October, Philippine Sugar Regulatory Administration head Wilson Gamboa said he had ordered traders and millers to import no more sugar for the next six months because of a glut.
Gamboa said the Philippines imported 1.23 million tonnes of from September 1995 to July 1996, resulting in an excess of 423,000 tonnes.
Zabaleta believes recent measures should be enough to stabilise prices.
Reductions on tariffs to ASEAN countries of 35 percent on refined sugar, which ended earlier this year, was a factor behind the glut, he said.
"There was a flurry of imports" before more favourable pricing mechanisms were ended, Zabaleta said.

Since then, he said that the Philippines has opted for a two-tier tariff system and set new quotas. "That being in place, we now feel comfortable there should not be any imports beyond the quota," he said. Zabaleta also said that there was a normal build-up of stocks during the harvest season.
"But the overhang should now be manageable with the quota system in place," he said.
The 300,000-tonne overhang could come down to 250,000 or even 200,000 towards the end of the crop year, Roxas and Zabaleta said.
Zabaleta said raw prices have recovered, but are still fluctuating. He said in dollar terms, prices were around 18 cents a pound, with a low of 16 and a high of 19 cents.
"We hope to see that (stabilise) with proper management. We'd like to see it (the price) at not less than 18 cents a pound," he said.
